raw_text:
### Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

#### Introduction
The exponential growth of transcatheter structural heart interventions, most notably transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), has highlighted the critical importance of secure large-bore vascular access [1,2]. While transfemoral (TF) arterial access remains the clinical gold standard due to its lower complication rates, approximately 5% to 10% of patients present with severe peripheral arterial disease (PAD), extensive calcification, or severe vessel tortuosity that precludes a standard transfemoral approach [3]. Historically, these patients required surgical intrathoracic alternative options, such as transapical or direct transaortic access, which are associated with elevated morbidity and prolonged recovery times. Over the past decade, percutaneous transcaval (caval-aortic) access has emerged as a highly effective, fully percutaneous alternative pathway for delivering large-bore devices directly to the aorta [4,5].

#### Anatomy and Physiology of Transcaval Access
The physiological foundation of transcaval access is inherently counterintestinal, yet elegant. It involves creating a temporary tract between the infrarenal inferior vena cava (IVC) and the adjacent abdominal aorta [4,5]. Although intentionally establishing an aortocaval communication would normally raise concerns of catastrophic retroperitoneal hemorrhage, the safety of this technique relies on a fundamental pressure gradient. Because the retroperitoneal space is a confined interstitial compartment, the ambient tissue pressure surrounding the tract exceeds the low venous pressure of the IVC [1]. Consequently, any arterial blood escaping the aortic puncture site is harmlessly decompressed into the low-pressure venous system of the IVC rather than extravasating into the retroperitoneum [8,17]. 

Pre-procedural planning is heavily reliant on multidetector computed tomography (CT) angiography [6]. Contrast-enhanced CT scans are utilized to identify a precise "transcaval window"—an infrarenal zone where the aorta and IVC are in close anatomical proximity, ideally free of interposed loops of bowel, major venous tributaries, or significant anterior aortic calcification [7].

#### Technical Execution and Electrosurgery
The technical success of the percutaneous transcaval approach is driven by transcatheter electrosurgical technique [8,9]. Under fluoroscopic guidance and using coplanar projections, a guiding catheter is advanced into the IVC and oriented toward the pre-planned target on the abdominal aorta [8,29]. A microcatheter carrying a stiff, polymer-jacketed guidewire is positioned at the catheter tip. By applying short bursts of radiofrequency energy (typically using an electrosurgical generator connected to the back end of the guidewire), the wire is energized to rapidly traverse the interstitial tissue barrier and enter the abdominal aorta [9]. Once access is confirmed, a loop snare previously positioned in the aorta captures the guidewire, allowing it to be exchanged for a high-strength, rigid support wire. A large-bore introducer sheath is then advanced across the vena cava and directly into the aorta, facilitating TAVR, mechanical circulatory support (MCS) such as the Impella 5.0/5.5, or thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) [10,11,12,13].

#### Vascular Closure and Long-Term Fate of the Tract
Upon completion of the primary intervention, the large-bore sheath is withdrawn, and the transcaval access tract must be securely closed. Currently, operators predominantly utilize off-label nitinol cardiac occluders, such as the Amplatzer Ductal Occluder (ADO), to plug the aortic hole [10,14,15]. Alternatively, dedicated, purpose-built percutaneous transcaval closure devices are being developed to streamline the process [15].

Safety and clinical feasibility have been rigorously evaluated in multicenter prospective trials, such as the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) transcaval trial [10]. This trial reported a high procedural success rate of 99%, with acceptable rates of major vascular complications and life-threatening bleeding given the extreme-risk cohort [10]. Follow-up at 12 months demonstrated a highly favorable long-term fate of these tracts, showing complete healing of the aortocaval channel in the vast majority of cases without evidence of late aortic dissection, pseudoaneurysm, or major retroperitoneal bleeding [16].

#### Comparative Clinical Efficacy and Guidelines
In contemporary practice, transcaval TAVR is often compared with other extrathoracic alternatives such as transaxillary/subclavian and transcarotid accesses [18,19,20]. Propensity-weighted analyses of Society of Thoracic Surgeons/American College of Cardiology (STS/ACC) TVT Registry data comparing transcaval and transaxillary TAVR revealed that transcaval access was associated with a significantly lower rate of stroke and transient ischemic attack [18], likely due to avoiding the manipulation of calcified supra-aortic vessels [21]. While surgical transcarotid access remains a highly viable non-femoral option with short ICU stays [22,23], systematic reviews and meta-analyses have consolidated the evidence, highlighting that transcaval TAVR represents a safe, non-thoracic pathway with comparable short- and long-term mortality [24,25,26].

Expert consensus guidelines, including the Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI) statements, emphasize the role of a dedicated Heart Team in vascular access decision-making [27,28]. Operators are encouraged to master these standardized procedures to expand their therapeutic armamentarium [27,29,30].

#### Conclusion
Transcaval access represents a paradigm shift in percutaneous large-bore vascular management. By exploiting retroperitoneal pressure dynamics and utilizing precise electrosurgical crossing, it provides a safe, highly reproducible, and fully percutaneous route to the abdominal aorta. Although technical proficiency and thorough CT planning are required, transcaval access is now established as a primary alternative strategy when transfemoral access is hostile, significantly improving clinical outcomes for sicker patient populations.
